cues.text: That instruction lives in the Boot ROM: a small program etched into the chip itself, when it was made. It can never be changed.

cues.text: That's its strength, and its weakness: if a flaw were ever found in a Boot ROM, no software update could fix it — only a new chip. So it's kept as small and simple as possible.

cues.text: But before it runs a single instruction of it, the Boot ROM checks its signature.

cues.text: Here's how. The code is run through a hash function, which boils it down to a short fingerprint.

cues.text: Change even a single bit, and the fingerprint changes completely.

cues.text: Apple signs that fingerprint with a private key that never leaves Apple. The public key in the Boot ROM can check the signature — but it can't forge one.

cues.text: That seal protects macOS itself. The operating system lives on a read-only volume, where every file has its own hash.

cues.text: Those hashes are hashed again, and again, all the way up a tree, into a single value: the seal.
